unit.title: Durable data and recovery
unit.summary: Keep saved data and pending edits intact when the app upgrades, retries, changes accounts, or cannot access storage.

lessons.title: Upgrade an old store while keeping its saved meaning
lessons.summary: Create data with the old model, upgrade it, and compare the saved fields. Keep a failed or unsupported source intact instead of treating it as empty.
objectives: Create and close a V1 SQLite fixture, migrate it, and check both accounts' complete saved values.
Explain inferred mappings, rename identity, versioned SwiftData schemas, and when a custom migration stage is needed.
Keep corrupt, unsupported, and unavailable sources intact while checking a separate Core Data candidate.
Name who controls cutover and recovery; distinguish JSON format checks from actual framework migrations.

sections.title: Begin with what the previous version saved
sections.html:
A migration converts saved data from an older model to the model the new app understands. Ask what the previous app actually wrote before testing the conversion. Room DAO tests can pass while an installed user's upgrade still loses data; a new current-model iOS store has the same blind spot. Sessions 053 and 083 introduced persistence and CRUD, meaning create, read, update, and delete. Here you write an older store, close its writer, migrate it, and read saved records through the destination model.

Our synthetic draft has an ID, account, and title. Version two renames title to displayTitle and adds origin with a historical value of legacy. Accounts A and B intentionally share the same draft ID. Acceptance requires both titles, both account identities, and both defaults to survive. Counting two rows alone is weak: an accidental cross-account overwrite or lost title could still produce the expected count. Write the expected projections before running the migration so the comparison cannot drift toward whatever the implementation happens to output.

Separate compatibility from business transformation. Renaming a field preserves the same meaning; splitting an address string into structured parts requires a domain rule. Neither is proven by incrementing a version integer. The companion's JSON journal upgrade tests a file format, CoreDataMigration.swift tests an actual Core Data SQLite store, and SwiftDataMigration.swift exercises a versioned framework schema. Keep three evidence rows instead of presenting one successful decoder as proof of all three. Every source is created beneath a caller-supplied temporary directory, with synthetic values.

sections.title: Keep the old model and identify renamed fields
sections.html:
A model describes a Core Data store's entities and attributes. Store metadata records information used to check compatibility with that model. This fixture supplies old and new NSManagedObjectModel objects directly rather than discovering compiled resources. A shipped app must package the required versions in the correct bundle. Check the built resources; a source .xcdatamodeld folder alone does not prove they are available. If the binary cannot read an installed version, report that boundary instead of creating an empty replacement.

The destination attribute's renamingIdentifier connects displayTitle to the historical title property. A required new field also needs a valid value for old records. In this fixture origin defaults to legacy, which means imported historical data rather than a false claim that the current application authored it. Keep the earlier canonical rename identity across successive renames. Removing an old property and adding an unrelated one can infer differently from the intended rename, so assert actual values after migration.

Core Data can infer a mapping for supported changes; inference success does not validate your product semantics. The fixture asks NSMappingModel for an inferred mapping, then gives it to NSMigrationManager. This is a real framework migration using an inferred mapping, rather than automatic source-model discovery during store opening. The checkout's CoreDataStore uses automatic migration and inference options instead. Both approaches require compatible source/destination definitions; this lab's explicit choice makes preservation and destination failure observable without changing the client.

let title = text(v2 ? "displayTitle" : "title")
if v2 { title.renamingIdentifier = "title" }
let origin = text("origin")
origin.defaultValue = "legacy"

This excerpt runs inside model(v2:) in the macOS companion, where text creates a required string attribute. The first line chooses a persisted property name. The second attaches migration identity only to the destination property. The third creates the added field; the fourth defines its historical default. Setting that default does not update an arbitrary live object or supply a server provenance guarantee. The complete file appends origin only to V2 and retains id/account unchanged.

The fixture retains string-based coordinator calls that resemble the inspected legacy checkout. Current Apple documentation deprecates the older metadataForPersistentStore(ofType:at:options:) overload in favor of the typed StoreType variant metadataForPersistentStore(type:at:options:), available from iOS 15 and macOS 12. That is an API modernization boundary, separate from a store-schema migration. The generic throwing performAndWait overload used by the host fixtures also needs iOS 15 or macOS 12; the full runner's macOS 14 floor covers it.

sections.title: Write a separate candidate and compare its records
sections.html:
A migration candidate is a converted store you have not yet chosen as authoritative. CoreDataMigration.swift first writes two drafts to a V1 SQLite store on a private context's queue. Its performAndWait closure performs the confined work synchronously: insert, save, then reset. The fixture removes the persistent store from its coordinator to close the writer. Only string projections leave the context. DELETE journaling simplifies comparison of the closed source file's bytes. It does not show that copying one file from a live WAL-backed database safely preserves its sidecars.

The migrate function reads metadata with a read-only option and checks the supplied source model. It obtains the inferred mapping and writes to a distinct destination URL. Afterward, rows opens the destination with the V2 model and verifies account, ID, title, and origin against the source projection. This offers a concrete rejection boundary: a candidate with incorrect meaning never replaces the old file. The lab deliberately stops before a production cutover because replacing a store while contexts or extensions still retain it is a separate ownership problem.

Read the central calls in order. The mapping call defines the conversion. The manager owns migration state for this attempt. migrateStore takes source URL/type/options and destination URL/type/options separately; its labels make an accidental source/destination swap reviewable. A throw must leave the application in a recoverable setup state. An error is neither an empty fetch nor proof that the source is disposable. There is no client database access in this program.

let mapping = try NSMappingModel.inferredMappingModel(
    forSourceModel: sourceModel, destinationModel: target)
let manager = NSMigrationManager(
    sourceModel: sourceModel, destinationModel: target)
try manager.migrateStore(
    from: source, sourceType: NSSQLiteStoreType,
    options: [NSReadOnlyPersistentStoreOption: true],
    with: mapping, toDestinationURL: destination,
    destinationType: NSSQLiteStoreType,
    destinationOptions: [NSSQLitePragmasOption: ["journal_mode": "DELETE"]])

The full fixture supplies every identifier above. These Apple-only calls require Core Data and a macOS SDK; the lab uses Swift 6 mode, with the exact compiler recorded in its README. Swift language mode and OS availability are different constraints. Core Data predates SwiftData, while the latter needs iOS 17 or macOS 14 and macro-capable tooling.

sections.title: Test SwiftData's own old-store upgrade path
sections.html:
A VersionedSchema names the persistent model types for one SwiftData version. The companion declares V1.Draft and V2.Draft separately, each with a Schema.Version. V2 connects displayTitle to its old title name using Attribute(originalName:) and gives origin a default. Plan lists both schemas and one lightweight migration stage. The V2 ModelContainer receives that plan and the same disk URL V1 wrote. Using an in-memory container or a different URL would create another store and bypass the installed-data question.

The first autoreleasepool scopes the old container and context. It disables autosave, inserts A and B, and explicitly saves. The second scope constructs the new container and fetches V2.Draft values. Account identity remains an ordinary field in this fixture, not framework authorization. The assertion compares complete sorted projections. Macro expansion, store construction, migration, and fetching can fail independently, so a compiler success alone cannot establish that this runtime preservation assertion passed.

For semantic transformations, SchemaMigrationPlan can use a custom MigrationStage with willMigrate and didMigrate callbacks. Treat those as stage-specific context work: arrange old-data preparation before the transition and new-model validation after it. Do not assume an old typed model remains queryable in the destination phase or that a closure offers both schemas simultaneously. A deduplication or required-field transformation needs its own old-store fixture and expected values. This companion verifies only its specified rename/default path; it is not a generic custom migration template.

Kotlin Room's exported schemas and migration tests are a useful comparison because they keep old definitions available and validate upgrades. The implementation boundary differs: Core Data maps managed object models, and SwiftData generates persistent model behavior. Direct SQL that is appropriate inside a Room migration is not a supported invitation to rewrite Core Data's private SQLite schema. Carry the preservation discipline across platforms, not the database implementation assumptions.

sections.title: Keep the source when an upgrade fails
sections.html:
A recovery policy says what remains available after a failed attempt and what can safely happen next. First classify the failure. Corrupt metadata cannot be read as the expected store. Unsupported metadata may describe a valid store this binary cannot interpret. Destination I/O failure may leave a partial candidate beside a healthy source. Protected-data unavailability can be temporary, while a missing model resource is a packaging defect. None of these is permission to erase unsent drafts and call a new empty store successful.

The Core Data fixture rejects a known SQLite store paired with the wrong source model, feeds invalid bytes to metadata inspection, and uses a regular file where the destination's parent directory should be. After each failure it verifies the source bytes and old-model rows remain available. The deliberate I/O failure is a deterministic test seam, not an actual measured disk-full event. JSON checks separately retain corrupt and future-version bytes. Record framework diagnostics without copying private data into learner evidence.

A real cutover needs one owner that excludes current contexts, other processes, and extension writers. Use framework-supported store replacement or a documented quiesced migration strategy, validate the candidate, and retain a recoverable original under the chosen retention/protection policy. Coordinate sidecars rather than renaming a single live SQLite file. A rollback binary may be unable to read V2, so retain a compatible restore path or use a forward repair. Source-code rollback alone does not undo persisted schema evolution.

Cancellation also has a boundary. Cancel before expensive work where possible; once framework migration is running, a Swift task cancellation flag is not automatically a framework cancellation request. NSMigrationManager exposes cancelMigration(withError:), but coordinating it requires retaining the correct manager and an explicit owner. This fixture is synchronous and does not claim to test mid-migration cancellation. If canceled or failed, do not publish the candidate, and keep the original until recovery is verified.

sections.title: Use the inspected store policy to ask preservation questions
sections.html:
A store-opening policy decides how the app reacts when opening fails. The inspected CoreDataStore.swift uses a main-queue context, automatic migration and mapping inference, and completeUnlessOpen protection. A caller-controlled branch removes the SQLite file and retries after an opening failure. That source observation shows a policy exists; it does not classify every stored value or justify using the branch for unsent drafts. The independent preservation fixture tests a different contract without changing the client or claiming its installed-store upgrades ran.

Review a proposed upgrade with four questions: which old models are supported, which meaning must survive, who owns quiescence/cutover, and how does a failed or interrupted attempt recover? Attach the synthetic expected projections and command results. Keep unsupported-version handling visible to the application owner. A release that cannot interpret future data should wait for a compatible binary or offer a reviewed export/repair route; it should not overwrite the evidence simply to reach the first screen.

quiz.question: Which fixture demonstrates Core Data migration?
options: Decode a JSON version integer into a new struct
Create/save/close a V1 SQLite store, migrate with Core Data, then fetch V2 values
Insert V2 objects into an in-memory store
quiz.explanation: The old framework store and destination model exercise metadata compatibility and mapping. JSON decoding and current-model CRUD test separate contracts.

quiz.question: The candidate opens but A's title became empty. Is the migration acceptable?
options: Yes, opening proves correctness
Yes, if the row count is unchanged
No, preservation includes domain values and account identity
quiz.explanation: Compatibility is weaker than preservation. Compare expected historical values, not just counts or successful construction.

quiz.question: An unsupported store is found during launch. What is the default for irreplaceable drafts?
options: Preserve it and report a compatible recovery path
Remove it and retry automatically
Interpret it as no saved drafts
quiz.explanation: Unknown compatibility is not absence or disposability. Keep the source and separate diagnosis, repair, and any explicitly authorized reset.

exercise.brief: Add an optional historical note to the scratch migration fixture. Check both accounts and reject a bad candidate while retaining the original store.
steps: Run the existing Core Data check in a fresh temporary directory and record the assertions that ran.
Add note to V1 and V2 with unchanged migration identity. Seed one nil value and one nonempty value.
Compare note along with the other fields. Reject a candidate when its saved values differ from the expected projection.
Run unsupported-model, corrupt-metadata, and destination-failure cases. Retain the source and describe who controls writer shutdown and cutover.
If SwiftData macro tooling is available, run that independent fixture and report its result separately.
acceptance: An actual V1 Core Data SQLite file exists before any V2 container is opened.
Both accounts, titles, defaults, and optional note states survive the accepted upgrade.
Rejected/corrupt/unsupported/I/O-failure cases preserve the source and never become empty success.
Evidence distinguishes host execution, SwiftData macro limitations, and pending device/cutover checks.
exercise.solution:
Preserve both a value and its deliberate absence. Create a string NSAttributeDescription named note, mark it isOptional = true, and add it to both models. Seed only B's note; leave A's nil. In rows, read the field inside performAndWait and represent nil with a fixed synthetic sentinel distinct from an empty string. Compare the complete A and B projections. The new origin default should become legacy without changing either note state. This tests more than a row count or a successful store open.

The accepted path still uses source metadata, inferred mapping, a distinct destination, and post-migration validation. For the rejected path, supply a deliberately wrong expected projection to an acceptance function after migration. That function throws a preservation error and does not invoke any replacement operation. Keep the original source URL untouched and refetch its old rows. Do not modify the old bytes to make the candidate assertion pass. The test distinguishes a framework-compatible candidate from one your product is prepared to publish.

Write the cutover answer as ordered ownership: stop scratch writers, close/reset contexts, validate the candidate and account-scoped invariants, perform a supported replacement only under the designated owner, reopen with the destination schema, then publish a ready state. If replacement or reopen fails, preserve diagnostics and use the retained old-store recovery procedure rather than silently constructing a new store. Define when retained sources are deleted and how their protection matches current data. The lab supplies preservation evidence but leaves process-death-at-cutover and device protection for a dedicated target test.

SwiftData uses the same optional-value fixture idea, but its schema declaration and migration plan remain separate source. Its macro helper may need the documented compiler flag inside this workspace sandbox. Record any compile or runtime failure honestly; a Core Data pass cannot substitute for a SwiftData pass. No exercise changes course progress or the client's persistent stores.

Android: Testing Room migrations and destructive fallback

repo.label: Observed store-open recovery and migration options
repo.why: The inspected remove-and-retry branch motivates explicit data classification; options at line 105 enable automatic inference but are not runtime preservation evidence.

checklist: I can prove an old store existed before migration.
I can explain rename/default preservation and framework boundaries.
I can retain corrupt or unsupported source data without empty success.
I can identify the owner of candidate validation and eventual cutover.

simple.story: A bakery keeps recipe cards in two drawers, A and B. Both drawers contain a card numbered 7. One says Tea Bread and the other says Seed Loaf. A new card design changes the label Title to Display Title and adds Origin. You copy the cards onto the new design and write legacy as their origin. Before putting them into use, you compare each drawer, number, and title with the originals. A tidy new design is useful only if the recipes still belong to the right drawers.
simple.meaning: A store migration changes the saved model while preserving the data's meaning. The Core Data fixture keeps the original store and validates a separate candidate. Account plus draft ID distinguishes the two records; rename identity preserves the title under its new property name.

example.before: V1 has A/draft-7/title = Tea Bread and B/draft-7/title = Seed Loaf. Neither row has an origin field.
example.change: Run the Core Data inferred mapping into a distinct V2 destination with displayTitle renamed from title and origin defaulted to legacy.
example.after: The V2 candidate has A/draft-7/displayTitle = Tea Bread/origin = legacy and B/draft-7/displayTitle = Seed Loaf/origin = legacy. Validate those projections; the original stays intact and cutover remains a separate step.

picture.caption: The Core Data preservation experiment closes V1, migrates into a separate V2 candidate, checks both account projections, and stops before production cutover.

items.label: Closed V1
items.text: The source contains two account-scoped drafts with the same draft ID.

items.label: Mapping
items.text: Rename title to displayTitle and give historical rows origin = legacy.

items.label: V2 candidate
items.text: Write the converted records to a distinct destination.

items.label: Compare
items.text: Check account, ID, title, and origin while retaining the original.

words.meaning: The definition of the stored entities, fields, and their rules.
Converting saved data from one supported model to another.
Information that connects a new property name to the same historical property.
A converted store being checked before it becomes the chosen store.
The selected saved fields compared to verify their meaning.
Switching the application to the accepted store under a designated owner.

simple.remember: Check an upgrade against actual old saved values, and keep the original until recovery is verified.
simple.boundary: Copying paper cards does not model Core Data contexts, SQLite sidecars, or SwiftData macros. The Core Data fixture uses a separate candidate; the SwiftData fixture reopens the same URL with its migration plan. A field named account does not enforce authorization. These checks do not verify production cutover or mid-migration cancellation.

lessons.title: Save offline edits and replay the same intent safely
lessons.summary: Save an edit with its pending command, reload it after restart, and handle lost replies, deletes, conflicts, and stale account results.
objectives: Save the local edit and its pending command through one durable boundary before publishing success.
Reload pending operations after process exit and reuse the same immutable operation ID.
Distinguish a lost response, a terminal conflict, a retry, and a retained delete marker.
Check account epoch when recording outcomes and explain why an actor does not coordinate other file writers.

sections.title: Save the edit and the pending command together
sections.html:
An outbox is a saved list of commands waiting for a service outcome. It must survive the screen and the process. An Android editor might write a Room row and schedule WorkManager, but a completed coroutine or Saved snackbar cannot join those operations automatically. If the process dies between the edit and queue insertion, an edit can be visible without a pending command. Reversing the order can leave a command without its recorded edit. The outbox pattern saves both through one persistence boundary.

Our synthetic example edits a card title. An account snapshot contains local records and an ordered array of commands. enqueue copies the snapshot, applies the local title or delete, appends the command, encodes everything, writes one file atomically, and only then advances actor memory. This is an intentionally small single-writer implementation. A transactional database can make the same domain promise across multiple rows; two separately written JSON files cannot be presented as one atomic transaction merely because both use atomic replacement.

Name two acknowledgments. Locally durable means the edit and command survived the local commit. Remotely accepted means the server applied or recognized the logical operation and the local acknowledgment persisted. Displaying one undifferentiated success hides the interesting recovery interval. The exercise labels pending, ambiguous and conflict explicitly. It avoids real bookings, payments, health data and networks; no success in this synthetic server establishes a production endpoint contract.

sections.title: Keep the same request identity when replaying
sections.html:
An operation ID names one logical intent, such as changing card r1 to Blue. Create it once and save it before sending. This command also stores the record ID, optional value, base revision, and delivery state. Base revision is the server version the edit expects. A nil value means delete in this fixture; it does not mean an omitted patch field. Restart, retry, refresh, and timeout keep the intent's ID. A new edit chosen after resolving a conflict gets a fresh ID and an appropriate revision precondition.

The synthetic server scopes receipts by account and operation ID and retains the immutable request fields. A replay with the same ID and payload returns its original outcome. Reusing the ID with a changed record, title or base revision throws identityReuse. Delivery state is client bookkeeping and is excluded from payload equivalence. The server writes its effect and receipt in one snapshot before returning. A server that writes them independently would have the same crash gap the outbox is intended to avoid.

Real idempotency requires a service agreement: authenticated account scope, payload binding, duplicate result behavior, retention window and concurrent-request handling. Local UUID generation alone cannot guarantee exactly one service effect. If a service expires its receipts before an offline client replays, the client needs reconciliation or a bounded operation-status lookup. This lab never expires receipts, making its assumptions visible. State the limits before using the pattern for any irreversible operation.

Java 11 Files.move with ATOMIC_MOVE illustrates a similar filesystem boundary: support depends on the provider and storage arrangement, and unsupported atomic movement throws. It does not turn several unrelated file operations into a database transaction. Foundation's atomic write is likewise a replacement facility, not an assertion that a remote server deduplicates or that power-loss persistence was measured.

sections.title: Publish the copied snapshot only after saving it
sections.html:
Enqueue means add a command to the saved pending list. DurableOutbox.enqueue checks cancellation and its ticket before copying the journal. A ticket carries account and epoch; the epoch identifies this account activation so older work can be rejected. validate also rejects the injected unavailable state. Copying values keeps the actor's acknowledged snapshot unchanged until persistence succeeds. The snippet belongs to the complete companion, where Command, Ticket, and Journal are defined; compile those files together rather than treating it as a standalone app.

try Task.checkCancellation()
try validate(ticket)
var next = journal
var account = next.accounts[ticket.account] ?? AccountState()
guard !account.commands.contains(where: { $0.id == command.id }) else {
    throw StoreFailure.duplicateOperation
}
account.records[command.record] = command.value
account.commands.append(command)
next.accounts[ticket.account] = account
try commit(next)

Task.checkCancellation rejects cooperative cancellation before this commit begins. The ticket is a value containing account and epoch. The dictionary lookup selects exactly that account; nil falls back only for a missing initialized account, never for failed disk decoding. The guard prevents duplicate pending IDs. Assigning an optional dictionary value removes the local record when nil, while the command still retains delete intent. append preserves FIFO order. Assigning the account back updates the copied journal. commit writes before publishing memory and contains no await.

A disk error therefore leaves this actor's old snapshot authoritative under the fixture policy. The UI can retain an unsaved edit separately and show a retryable failure. Atomic replacement limits partial destination exposure, but the companion does not call fsync or simulate sudden power loss. Large synchronous encodes/writes also occupy the actor's executor while they run. A production store needs bounded batches and a suitable I/O owner; moving blocking work into an actor does not make it nonblocking.

An actor isolates access to its own state; it does not supply a dedicated disk thread. This fixture's commit has no await, so another call to the same actor cannot interleave between its final check, synchronous write, and memory publication. Other actors or processes can still write the path unless you prevent that separately. For production work, lesson 088 describes a bounded blocking-I/O worker. Offloading introduces a suspension. Coordinate account transitions and the actual write order with that worker, then revalidate before publication. A post-write guard alone cannot undo bytes already saved under an obsolete command. An unowned Task.detached does not establish any of those rules. No throughput improvement has been measured here.

sections.title: Resolve a missing reply without inventing another operation
sections.html:
An ambiguous outcome means the client lacks a reliable answer about a request that may already have taken effect. RestartProbe creates that gap deliberately. Its seed process saves a command, sends it to the disk-backed synthetic server, and loses the reply after the server saves its effect. The outbox marks the command ambiguous and exits. A new process reloads both files, activates the account with a new epoch, and replays the same command. The persisted receipt returns accepted, the outbox saves removal, and the server's effect counter stays one.

This proves a bounded ordinary-exit/restart scenario. It does not reproduce a kernel crash, an abrupt kill during replacement, receipt expiry or a real HTTP exchange. The effect count is a deterministic assertion, not a performance measurement. A different gap also matters: the server can acknowledge while the outbox's removal write fails. Keep the old command because the acknowledgment is not locally durable; replay then resolves it through the same service identity.

Replay captures the ticket and commands, checks cancellation, applies the synthetic request, checks cancellation again and records the outcome. The await admits account transitions between send and acknowledgment. record validates the ticket inside the actor turn that mutates the journal. A late A response after A-to-B-to-A cannot acknowledge a command under A's newer activation. The service may already have changed A; local freshness cannot retract that effect. Recovery belongs to A's retained intent and receipt, never B's visible state.

Cancellation after sending is similarly not evidence of server rollback. In the fixture, a cancellation check after the server call leaves the command pending. A subsequent authorized replay asks the server to resolve it. This is why canceling a screen and deleting a durable operation must be separate product decisions. The next lesson adds credential ownership without converting cancellation into a new operation identity.

sections.title: Retain deletion evidence and pause on conflict
sections.html:
A tombstone is retained evidence of deletion. Here the server keeps the record's ID, newer revision, and nil value after a delete. The local command also keeps its record ID and base revision after the visible dictionary entry disappears. That allows replay to deliver the delete and prevents an update expecting revision zero from silently restoring a newer deleted value. A production retention policy must account for offline duration and reconciliation; removing tombstones immediately can make stale requests look like legitimate creates.

Revision mismatch yields conflict. The server persists that outcome under the operation ID, and the outbox marks the command conflict without removing it. The one-pass scheduler stops the account FIFO at that point. This is conservative: even independent records wait behind a conflicting predecessor. Per-record lanes can improve throughput, but require explicit dependency rules and stable ordering. Do not add arbitrary concurrency until the meaning of a delete followed by recreate, or two edits to one record, is clear.

Rebasing means creating a new request against a newer known server revision. The replacement needs a fresh operation ID because the old ID remains bound to the rejected payload and outcome. The supplied resolver supports one pending command for that record and replaces it in the same queue slot. It rejects a second dependent edit without changing bytes or memory. Supporting a whole lane requires an atomic policy for all dependent values and revision preconditions; removing the head and appending its replacement can reorder intent. Keep-server, merge, or discard are separate domain choices. A caller's current revision can also become stale before delivery. The fixture does not implement automatic merge or a general dependency resolver.

Android WorkManager can schedule retryable background work, but it does not supply the outbox transaction or server conflict policy. iOS background execution has different grants and lifetimes; foreground replay or a granted background task can call the same repository scheduler. The durable queue must remain correct when no grant arrives. This unit does not implement CloudKit, multi-device merge engines, APNs wakeups or a guarantee of continuous background synchronization.

sections.title: Load truthfully before allowing the next write
sections.html:
A load result must say whether saved intent exists and whether it can be read. AtomicDisk treats only the expected missing-file Cocoa error as absence. Invalid contents become corrupt; an unknown future format becomes unsupported. Permission and other read failures propagate. Returning an empty list for every read error would allow a later write to replace commands you could not read. The decoder also rejects duplicate pending IDs, checking one meaning rule beyond valid JSON syntax.

Account activation rotates a persisted epoch and retains each account's records separately. This is one process owning a synthetic file, not a cross-process locking scheme. Constructing two writable outbox actors for the same path can cause lost updates even though each actor serializes itself. An extension or another process needs a shared transaction owner, database coordination or a deliberately reviewed communication boundary. Tests instantiate replacement actors sequentially to model reload rather than authorize concurrent writers.

The checkout's MedicationReminderStore shows atomic file writing and distinguishes missing from corrupt data, while CredentialManagerActor preserves a credential generation across async work. These inspected seams motivate the lab; they do not prove the client has this outbox or server receipt API. Audit request payload authorization, cleanup failures, storage protection and backup retention separately when proposing a real feature. An account-specific local path is helpful but cannot enforce server resource authorization.

quiz.question: The server committed a command but the response was lost. Which replay is defensible?
options: Generate a new operation ID
Retain the original command and use the verified server idempotency contract
Delete the command because cancellation proves rollback
quiz.explanation: Ambiguous outcome means the effect may exist. A stable account-scoped ID and immutable payload let the service recognize the original effect.

quiz.question: Why put the local edit and pending intent in the same snapshot?
options: To avoid a crash gap between two separate durable writes
To make every request exactly once without server support
To permit unrelated processes to write the same JSON file
quiz.explanation: One persistence boundary joins the local state and intent. It supplies neither remote deduplication nor cross-process coordination.

quiz.question: A command conflicts at revision 4. What should a rebased edit do?
options: Reuse the old ID with a changed payload
Silently clear the server revision
Use a new logical operation ID and the reviewed current precondition
quiz.explanation: An idempotency identity binds immutable intent. Rebase changes that intent and needs a new command; conflict resolution remains domain policy.

quiz.question: A conflicted edit has a later pending edit to the same record. Which resolution preserves a defensible ordering contract?
options: Remove the conflict and append its replacement behind the later edit.
Reuse the rejected operation ID with the latest payload.
Reconcile dependent intents and preconditions atomically, or reject the case under an explicit one-pending-command limit.
quiz.explanation: Moving the replacement behind dependent work can change intent order and make its base revision stale. The supplied bounded resolver rejects multiple pending commands for the record; a broader resolver needs an explicit dependency policy and atomic persistence.

exercise.brief: Add or independently reproduce bounded conflict resolution in the scratch outbox. Keep deletes, recreation, queue order, and accounts correct across restart.
steps: Run HostChecks and both RestartProbe modes in fresh isolated directories. Record each actual result.
Seed an accepted create, then queue a delete using the correct base revision. Reload before replay.
Queue a stale edit and check that its conflict stops FIFO replay before later work is acknowledged.

For resolveConflict, require one pending command for the record. Replace the conflict in its existing slot with a fresh ID. Reject dependent edits unless one explicit atomic policy reconciles them all.
Switch A to B to A between send and acknowledgment. Record the remote effect separately from the rejected stale local commit.
acceptance: Ordinary process restart reloads pending intent and stable operation identity.
A lost response plus replay creates one synthetic server effect, including after receipt reload.
Delete intent outlives the removed local row; stale updates cannot resurrect it automatically.

Rebase has a fresh ID, preserves its queue position and commits queue/local state together; multiple pending edits to its record are rejected without changing bytes, and unrelated accounts remain unchanged.
Disk/cancellation/conflict failures remain distinct and no device/background/production behavior is claimed.
exercise.solution:
Resolve one conflicted intent without moving it behind later work. The supplied reference validates cancellation and the account ticket, finds an entry marked conflict, and requires exactly one pending command for that record. It copies the journal, replaces the entry at its existing index with a fresh ID and supplied current revision, updates the copied optimistic record, and commits once. With two edits for that record, it throws dependentCommands before changing disk or memory. Removing and appending could let the later edit run first and advance the server revision. Supporting that case requires an explicit atomic reconciliation of every dependent intent and precondition.

HostChecks.rebaseChecks demonstrates both schedules. One conflicted edit is replaced in its original slot, its fresh ID produces one additional server effect, and its original receipt remains conflict. In the two-command fixture, the head conflicts while the later edit targets the current revision. Resolution is rejected, the complete queue and its file bytes stay unchanged, and FIFO replay produces no later effect. An injected failed write also preserves the original conflict. These checks establish the bounded local policy; a supplied current revision can still become stale before a real server receives the replacement.

For the delete/recreate answer, the original create uses revision zero, the accepted delete uses revision one, and an explicit recreate uses revision two because the synthetic tombstone still carries the newer revision. The recreate is a new user intent with a fresh operation ID. Replay the queued delete before recreating, or define the dependency as a single ordered lane. Assert the server value is nil after delete acknowledgment and only becomes the chosen new title after the new command is accepted.

Use the manual acknowledgment seam for the account schedule: capture A's ticket, send the command to the synthetic server, activate B, activate A again, and call record with the old ticket. staleAccount is the expected local result. Fetch B through its own current activation and verify its records remain unrelated. Then reactivate A, replay its retained pending command, and resolve the existing server receipt without another effect. This proves ownership at the local commit boundary rather than pretending the first service effect disappeared.

Finally, preserve the original before-image file for an injected RejectingDisk test. Both the bytes and a same-actor read must still reflect the acknowledged state after failure. Keep the ordinary restart proof and these injected failure proofs in separate evidence rows. A crash during rename, actual disk exhaustion, scheduler grants and receipt-retention negotiation remain further verification, with no automatic learner completion.

checklist: I can distinguish local durability and remote acceptance.
I can retain intent after an ambiguous outcome or cancellation.
I can explain stable identity, deletion and conflict retention.
I can reject stale account acknowledgment at the actual commit.

simple.story: You order one blue mug from a shop. Before sending the order, you write order 7 in your notebook beside the mug you chose. The shop packs it and keeps receipt 7, but its reply never reaches you. Next morning, your notebook still says the reply is missing. You ask again using order 7. The shop finds its receipt and answers without packing another mug. You cross the pending order off only after recording that answer. Forgetting the reply did not mean the first order failed.
simple.meaning: An outbox saves the local edit and its pending command together. A stable operation ID lets a cooperating server recognize replay after a lost response. Acknowledgment removes the command only after that local change is saved.

example.before: After a sequential reload and activation of A with a fresh epoch, local card r1 = Blue and pending op-7 is ambiguous. The saved synthetic server receipt accepts op-7; effects = 1.
example.change: Replay the unchanged op-7 request under A's current ticket.
example.after: The server returns its saved receipt, effects stays 1, and the outbox saves removal of op-7. A's local r1 remains Blue. This is the ordinary-restart fixture contract, not a power-loss or network measurement.

picture.caption: A lost reply leaves op-7 pending; replay reuses the saved server receipt so the effect count stays 1 and acknowledgment can be saved locally.

items.label: Local commit
items.text: Save r1 = Blue and command op-7 in one snapshot.

items.label: Server commit
items.text: Save one effect and its op-7 receipt before replying.

items.label: Lost reply
items.text: Keep op-7 pending with an ambiguous outcome.

items.label: Replay
items.text: Read the existing receipt and save local acknowledgment without another effect.

A stable identity for one logical intent, reused across its delivery attempts.
The server's saved request identity and outcome used to recognize a replay.
The client does not know whether the server applied the request.
A retained deletion record, including revision, that helps reject stale updates.

simple.boundary: The shop analogy assumes a server that binds receipts to account, immutable payload, and operation ID. Real receipt retention and concurrency need a service contract. The actor isolates its own state; it is not a dedicated I/O thread or a lock for other actors or processes. Atomic replacement does not prove power-loss durability. Dependent edits need an explicit atomic reconciliation policy.

lessons.title: Keep login and refresh results with the current session
lessons.summary: Use a synthetic login flow to check callbacks, refresh, storage failure, and logout. Explain Keychain policy without treating fake-vault checks as device evidence.
objectives: Check callback destination and state, then redeem a one-time code with its matching PKCE verifier.
Reject a login or refresh result whose epoch became stale while the operation was waiting.
Choose narrow Keychain item identity and accessibility; give different OSStatus failures different recovery paths.
Report fake-provider checks separately from browser presentation, signed Keychain behavior, passkeys, and real-provider verification.

sections.title: Give the login attempt and its result an owner
sections.html:
An authentication owner keeps track of the pending attempt, credentials, and when those credentials may become current. An Android app using a Custom Tab and an OAuth library still needs that owner. iOS needs it too, with different presentation and storage APIs. Sessions 018 and 054 introduced refresh and system web authentication. Here an executable synthetic provider joins those state transitions so a successful callback can still be rejected if the account session has changed.

MockAuth.swift has three distinct owners. AuthSession retains the pending attempt, current credential view and epoch. MockProvider issues one-time synthetic authorization codes and rotates synthetic refresh tokens. FakeVault represents a fallible credential store without calling Security services. The host checks drive login, refresh, failed deletion and a late completion in an explicit order. No browser is launched, no HTTP request is sent, no real identity claims are processed and no Keychain item is changed.

Define the application state in product terms: signed out, authorization pending, exchange pending, signed in, refresh pending, temporarily unavailable and cleanup pending. These states are not all stored as an enum in the compact fixture, but they define its observable transitions. A denied exchange returns to a recoverable login outcome; a temporarily locked vault cannot be treated as a valid durable session. A late credential result must pass ownership before becoming visible. An authorization code is not itself an account identity or resource permission.

sections.title: Use state to match the attempt and PKCE to bind code redemption
sections.html:
State is an OAuth value used to match a callback to the pending attempt. PKCE is proof key for code exchange: it binds redemption of an authorization code to that attempt's verifier. The attempt also carries an epoch, the session freshness value. Check the callback's destination and require unambiguous query fields as well as matching state. The synthetic provider saves a challenge with its one-time code and checks the submitted verifier's challenge during exchange. State and PKCE protect different relationships; one cannot replace the other.

For S256, the companion hashes the verifier's UTF-8 bytes with CryptoKit SHA256 and encodes the digest using base64url without padding. Its host assertion uses the published RFC 7636 example vector to catch encoding mistakes. A SHA256 call does not generate entropy. The fixture deliberately receives a fixed test verifier and state so failures are repeatable; neither these constants nor its synthetic token generation should be copied into a real provider integration.

Production attempt material must come from cryptographically suitable randomness, remain scoped to one attempt, meet the provider's protocol requirements, and never appear in logs or URLs beyond the fields intended by the protocol. The verifier is submitted at exchange, while the challenge travels at authorization. A packaged client secret is not confidential merely because it is absent from source control. Use a reviewed public-client flow and an appropriate provider/library instead of treating this lab as a security implementation.

The following host function is complete once Foundation and CryptoKit are imported. Data wraps the digest bytes. base64EncodedString supplies standard base64; the three replacements convert its alphabet and remove padding. These lines establish the encoding calculation used by the fake provider, not the correctness of a remote server's validation or of random generation.

func s256(_ verifier: String) -> String {
    Data(SHA256.hash(data: Data(verifier.utf8))).base64EncodedString()
        .replacingOccurrences(of: "+", with: "-")
        .replacingOccurrences(of: "/", with: "_")
        .replacingOccurrences(of: "=", with: "")
}

CryptoKit requires supported Apple platforms, including iOS 13 or macOS 10.15 for these basic APIs; the companion is compiled with the installed macOS SDK in Swift 6 mode. A language-mode selection is not an availability check. Other platforms need their own cryptographic adapter and verification rather than a handwritten digest.

sections.title: Validate the callback before awaiting the exchange
sections.html:
A callback is the returned URL carrying the synthetic authorization result. acceptCallback first checks that the pending attempt and current epoch match. URLComponents separates the URL into fields. The fixture requires its exact scheme, host, and callback path, rejects user information, port, and fragment, and requires exactly one state and one nonempty code. Duplicate fields are rejected so two parsers cannot disagree about which value counts. A real adapter also needs the provider's documented error, issuer, and redirect rules; this fake checks only its stated success shape.

After acceptance, pending becomes nil before exchange. Replaying the callback therefore cannot cause another accepted attempt. login awaits the provider's code exchange, then calls install with the captured epoch. An account transition can occur during that await. install checks cancellation and epoch, writes the fake vault, and publishes current only after storage succeeds. No await separates the last ownership check and fake-vault update in this compact actor method.

The host check returns a wrong-state callback, a duplicate-state callback and then a valid one. A rejection does not install credentials. The provider consumes an authorization code only after validating its verifier, and later reuse is denied. A callback failure, provider denial, cancellation and credential-storage failure are separate outcomes. Do not repeatedly open authentication UI from a generic catch branch; give the person an explicit retry or cancel action.

In a real iOS target, retain ASWebAuthenticationSession and its presentation-context owner, start it from the intended scene, and handle failed start separately from user cancellation. It is a platform browser flow, not a fake URLComponents function. ASWebAuthenticationSession starts at iOS 12, with later callback APIs requiring their own availability checks. This lab leaves actual scene presentation, browser cancellation, redirect registration and provider interoperability unexecuted.

sections.title: Treat refresh, local logout, and cleanup as separate outcomes
sections.html:
Refresh exchanges an existing refresh token for new credentials. This synthetic provider consumes the old token and issues a new one. AuthSession captures its epoch before awaiting the provider, then uses the login installation guard again. The checked happy path has one refresh caller at a time. The actor declaration does not make that single-flight, meaning one shared operation joined by several callers: await allows other calls to enter. This fixture does not coalesce simultaneous refreshes. Session 018 and the client's credential owner supply the broader ownership context.

A production account service normally owns one refresh operation that callers join. Individual waiter cancellation need not cancel work still needed by other requests, while logout cancels or invalidates the whole account operation. Keep a refresh generation as well as account epoch if newer refreshes can supersede older ones. Refresh requests must avoid recursively entering credential adaptation. Replaying the original business request after refresh must retain its original idempotency identity and its replayable body.

Logout immediately invalidates epoch and pending attempt and clears the current in-memory credential. It marks cleanupPending before asking the fake vault to delete. If deletion fails, local authorization remains closed and the cleanup obligation remains visible. The host holds a provider result, performs logout with injected deletion denial, then tries installing that old result. The stale guard rejects it. RetryCleanup can finish the failed deletion without making the old session current.

The fixture's vault and cleanup marker are memory-only. It therefore does not prove logout survives a process restart with failed Keychain deletion. A real implementation needs a durable, correctly protected sign-out marker or another explicit policy that prevents old vault material from being loaded while cleanup is pending. Server revocation is also independent of local deletion and may fail offline. Record these obligations as residual recovery work, not as reasons to claim logout completed globally.

Token rotation means replacing the old refresh token with a new one. It creates another failure boundary: the provider can consume the old token before FakeVault.save rejects the new token. current then still holds the old credential view, but its refresh token is no longer usable. The recorded HostChecks schedule injects that locked-save failure, checks that a plain retry after unlock is denied, and recovers with logout and a new synthetic login. This provider offers no reconciliation API or rotation grace period. A real provider may document those alternatives; a generic retry does not create them. The existing shared-refresh workbench explains a possible coalescing ownership pattern, which this companion neither implements nor verifies.

sections.title: Choose exactly which secret item can be used and when
sections.html:
A Keychain query describes the secret item an operation should match. ProtectedDataExercise.swift constructs a generic-password query for one synthetic service and account. It sets synchronizable to false and chooses WhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly accessibility. The host KeychainChecks inspects that dictionary and its status policy without calling SecItem APIs. Dictionary construction checks configuration values; it does not prove a signed iOS target can add, read, update, or delete an item. Access-group and entitlement behavior still need their own target evidence.

WhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly limits access to unlocked use and prevents migration to a different restored device. AfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly permits availability after the first unlock following reboot, including later locked periods, while retaining the device-only restoration boundary. Choosing between them is a product availability decision. State whether background replay actually needs credentials while locked; do not weaken all secrets to make one retry work. Default accessibility and an explicitly chosen policy should not be confused with passkey storage or Secure Enclave key generation.

A production adapter distinguishes a lookup identity from insertion attributes and update values. Match the intended class/service/account/access group, request only necessary results, update existing data, and add only on a reviewed item-not-found path. A duplicate add can occur under competing writers and needs bounded reconciliation. Deletion should be narrowly scoped and usually treat not-found as already absent under its contract. Never use a class-only delete to clean up this exercise.

The inspected KeychainManager matches service and account, updates first, and attempts add when the update adapter reports either itemNotFound or notAvailable. Its error adapter gives those statuses distinct cases. This is the checkout's legacy control flow, not the recovery policy recommended above. notAvailable does not establish that an item is absent, so review that fallback and the callers' availability requirements independently. Source inspection does not prove signed-device behavior or successful logout cleanup. The lab does not call this wrapper or its broad test-only deletion helper.

sections.title: Give absence and unavailable access different recovery paths
sections.html:
OSStatus is the result code from a Security operation. errSecItemNotFound says no item matched that specific query; it cannot tell you whether you chose the wrong service or account. errSecInteractionNotAllowed says required interaction is unavailable in the operation's context. Deferring or returning to the foreground may be appropriate; deleting is not an automatic response. errSecNotAvailable is also different from absence. Entitlement and parameter errors need configuration repair. Keep bounded status diagnostics without secret data or full query values.

The companion maps those statuses into success, absent, deferUntilAvailable, duplicate, configuration and other. This is an application policy, not a promise that every interaction-not-allowed result means the device is locked. A device observation can guide when to retry, but the actual Keychain call remains fallible. Session 100 connects this distinction to protected files and process recovery. A fake locked flag tests the application's reaction only.

Android Keystore and iOS Keychain are related facilities with different storage and access contracts: Keystore commonly owns cryptographic keys, whereas Keychain can store password-like items under system policies. A bearer token in Keychain is not automatically a Secure Enclave key. Java synchronized or a Kotlin Mutex can serialize wrapper state, but neither resolves server rotation, stale account completion or restoration policy. Carry ownership tests across platforms and verify their actual storage APIs independently.

sections.title: Require server verification before installing a passkey-based session
sections.html:
A relying party is the service that verifies a public-key credential response. A passkey flow uses AuthenticationServices requests, a server challenge, relying-party configuration, and server verification. It is not a refresh-token string in a generic-password Keychain item. The app needs associated-domain setup and a presentation owner for the intended scene. Signed-target and controlled-service checks establish those boundaries. Even a successful platform callback must pass server verification and current account ownership before the app installs its resulting session.

This lesson does not create passkeys, register an associated domain, authenticate an account or evaluate biometric policy. The exercise asks you to identify the seam where a verified passkey result could enter the existing session owner, with the same epoch and durable credential rules. Passwordless sign-in, OAuth authorization and bearer-token storage can participate in one product, but their proofs stay separate.

quiz.question: What does PKCE S256 prove in this synthetic exchange?
options: That fixed state is secure in production
That the exchanged verifier matches the challenge bound to the code
That the user owns every requested resource
quiz.explanation: PKCE binds code redemption to the verifier. Attempt state, entropy, identity verification and server authorization remain separate responsibilities.

quiz.question: A valid exchange completes after logout. What allows installation?
options: Successful exchange alone
The old callback's correct state alone
A current epoch and successful vault commit; the old epoch must fail
quiz.explanation: Protocol success does not restore ownership. The final commit guard rejects old login/refresh results after logout.

quiz.question: The vault returns errSecInteractionNotAllowed. Should the adapter clear credentials as missing?
options: No, preserve the unavailable/error state and apply a bounded recovery policy
Yes, every non-success is item-not-found
Yes, if the code runs in an actor
quiz.explanation: Interaction restrictions and absence are different. Actor serialization does not make Security access available or erase its OSStatus contract.

exercise.brief: In the mock flow, deny one refresh and add an explicit recovery state. Write a narrow Keychain and background-access policy using synthetic data.
steps: Run the RFC S256 vector and the existing synthetic login, refresh, logout, and vault checks.
Add a test-only provider switch that denies one refresh. Check that it publishes no new credentials.
Hold an exchange result, start another attempt or log out, then try installing the result under its old epoch.
Inject locked-save and deletion failures. Check that cleanup stays visible and stale installation fails.
Write policies for Keychain accessibility, status recovery, shared refresh, and durable sign-out. Name where server-verified passkey results would enter.
acceptance: Wrong or duplicate state, code reuse, and old epochs never publish credentials.
A failed vault write cannot be described as a durable authenticated session.
Logout closes local authorization even when deletion fails, and the remaining cleanup is explicit.
The policy separates synthetic execution from browser, Keychain, passkey and real-provider evidence.
exercise.solution:
Make the denial happen at one named boundary. Add a test-only failNextRefresh property and an enabling method to MockProvider. Check it before consuming the old token, clear it, and throw a typed synthetic denial. Capture current credentials, attempt refresh, assert the denial, and check that current stayed unchanged. This is a pre-rotation fixture choice, not proof of every provider's failure behavior. Choose the retry policy explicitly. Investigating rotation that succeeded before a lost response needs a separate ambiguity fixture.

Use the manual install seam to order stale outcomes without sleeps. Begin attempt A, obtain its provider result, begin B or logout, then call install with A's epoch. Expect stale and inspect the current state. In the deletion-denied schedule, current must be nil while cleanupPending remains true. Clear the fake denial, call retryCleanup, and assert the obligation ends. This demonstrates local state recovery; it deliberately does not persist the marker or read surviving Keychain material after restart.

The adapter policy chooses foreground-only device-only accessibility for this synthetic editor and accepts reauthentication after restoration to another device. If background credentials become a requirement, justify the after-first-unlock alternative and verify before-first-unlock behavior on a signed device. Treat not-found as absence, interaction restrictions as unavailable, duplicate add as bounded update/requery, and entitlement/parameter failures as configuration. Keep the query identity narrow on every operation and retain no real secrets in learner artifacts.

Finally, describe one shared refresh operation with waiter cancellation and account invalidation as separate inputs, and a durable sign-out marker consulted before credential reload. For passkeys, place server-verified challenge results upstream of session installation; keep browser, relying-party association and signature verification outside the fake provider's proof. The finished exercise is a reviewable mock extension and recovery policy, not a production authentication certification.

I can reject late credentials after logout.
